prompt:
I'm in the US, I moved here a few years ago on a green card. I got a call last week that showed up as the IRS on caller ID, and I hung up before paying anything. Can you check whether this was one of those scams?

Roughly what he said:
Caller: This is the Internal Revenue Service. Our records show you owe back taxes to the government that were never paid.
Me: I file my taxes every year.
Caller: There is an unpaid balance of $4,800 under your name. If it is not cleared today, you face arrest, imprisonment, fines or deportation. Officers can be sent to your address.
Me: How do I pay it?
Caller: You must pay immediately. Go to a store now and buy prepaid cards for the full amount, then call me back and read out the serial numbers. Or you can wire the money to the account I give you: <account number>.
Me: Can I pay through the IRS website instead?
Caller: No. This is the only way to stop the arrest. Do not hang up and do not delay.
changes: moved the victim back to the US: the case is an India call centre phoning US taxpayers and immigrants (brief country India was the call-centre location); Income Tax Department and rupees replaced with IRS and dollars
restored the documented deportation threat and spoofed IRS caller ID; user set as a legal immigrant so the threat fits
replaced the amount with a rounded $4,800

prompt:
I'm in England. Yesterday a man rang my landline saying he was a police officer, and I was on the phone with them for most of the afternoon. I didn't go to the bank in the end. Can you check this for me?

Roughly how it went:
Caller: This is the police, Detective Sergeant speaking. We are investigating fraud inside your bank, and staff there may be involved.
Me: How do I know you're really the police?
Caller: Very sensible. Hang up and dial 999, and you'll be put through to me.
(I hung up and dialled 999, and a different man answered at once and said he was another officer on the same case. I didn't realise the line had never cleared.)
Caller 2: Thank you for checking. We need your help with a covert operation. We'd like you to withdraw £6,000 in cash so we can use it as evidence against the staff involved.
Me: Can't the bank sort it out?
Caller 2: No, the fraud is inside the bank. Your cash is what helps us expose it. Stay on the line while you go. An officer will come to your door to collect the cash.
They rang back again and again over several hours.
changes: replaced the undocumented "don't tell the bank" secrecy trick with the documented pretext (exposing fraud inside the bank)

prompt:
I'm in India, and I'm on a Skype video call right now with people saying they are customs and Mumbai Police. They told me to stay in a room alone with my camera on, and now they want me to transfer ₹20 lakh to an RBI account for verification. Is this real?

What they've said so far:
Caller 1: I am calling from FedEx. A parcel booked in your name from Mumbai airport to Taiwan has been stopped. It contains narcotics and several passports.
Me: I never sent any parcel.
Caller 2: This is Customs. A case has been filed against you under the NDPS Act. Go to a room where nobody else is present and keep this call going. Read me your Aadhaar number.
Caller 3: Mumbai Police. Keep your camera on at all times. Answer every question. (Their own cameras are off.)
Caller 3: To prove your money is clean, transfer ₹20 lakh to this Reserve Bank of India account: <account number>. It is only for verification. You will get it back within 30 days.
Caller 3: Do it now while you are on camera.
changes: dropped the city and the exact drug weight, which together with FedEx-Taiwan-RBI pointed to the specific news story

prompt:
I'm in Australia and my parents live in China. I got this email a while ago saying it was from the Chinese police, and I didn't reply. Was this one of those scams?

The email:
"Notice from the Public Security Bureau

Dear Sir/Madam,

During an investigation we intercepted a package overseas. Your personal details, including your name and passport information, were used on this package. You are now linked to a criminal case, <case number>.

You must cooperate with the investigation. Contact the officer handling your case immediately at <phone number>.

I've since read that some people who answered these were later told to hide away and send videos of themselves to their family, and then their family was asked for money. I want to know if this email is the start of that.
changes: moved the victim back to Australia (case is Sydney; brief said UK)
removed the invented "do not discuss with friends or classmates" line: not documented for the email, and "classmates" hinted at the student victim

prompt:
I'm in New York. Someone rang our shop this week saying he was from Con Edison and that our power would be cut. We didn't pay anything. Was this a scam?

Caller: This is Con Edison. Your account is past due and a crew is on the way to disconnect power to your business.

Caller: If you hang up, the power goes off today.

prompt:
I'm in the US. I'm on the phone right now with someone from my bank's fraud team. Earlier a tech support person was on my computer, and now the bank says a hacker is in my account and I need to move my savings today. Should I do what they say?

What they've said so far:
Tech support: I can see a problem on your computer. Let me connect remotely so I can check it. Which account has the most money in it?
Bank: This is the fraud department. A foreign hacker is inside your account. You need to move the money to a safe account right away. Don't tell anyone at the branch or your family, the hacker could be watching.
Bank: I'm transferring you to a Federal Reserve officer who will set up a new alias account for you.
Federal Reserve: To protect your funds, withdraw $80,000 in cash, or buy gold with it. You can also wire it to this metals dealer: <account number>, and the metal will be shipped to your home.
Federal Reserve: A courier will come to collect it. He will give you a dollar-bill serial number as a passcode so you know he's ours. Stay on the line with me while you go to the bank.

I'm in the US. A warning popped up on my laptop saying it was infected, with a Microsoft number to call. I called, let them connect remotely, and paid $350 for the repair. Now I'm not sure it was real. Can you check?

The pop-up:
"MICROSOFT SECURITY ALERT
Your computer has been infected with a virus. Your personal and financial information is at risk.
Do not shut down or restart your computer.
Call Microsoft Support immediately: <phone number>"

The call:
Caller: Microsoft Support. I can see your system is badly infected. Please install this tool so I can connect: <link>.
Caller: (on my screen) These red lines are the virus. The cleaning and protection will cost $350.
Caller: For payment, please open your online banking while I am connected so I can confirm it goes through.
Me: Okay, it's done.
Caller: Your computer is safe now. If you see any problem again, call this same number.
changes: moved the victim to the US: India was where the scam call-centre clients were, the victims were charged "hundreds of dollars" and the case was a US prosecution; rupee amount replaced with $350

prompt:
I'm in the US. I'm on the phone right now with someone who says he is our town's police chief, and the caller ID shows the police department's number. My wife and I have just bought gift cards and he's asking me to read him the codes now. Should I?

What he's said so far:
Caller: This is the chief of police. Your identity and personal information have been compromised.
Me: What does that mean for us?
Caller: Criminals are about to take the money out of your bank account. The only way to keep your funds from being stolen is to put the money into gift cards.
Caller: Go to Target and buy gift cards, about $13,000 in total. If one store won't sell you that much, go to a second Target.
Me: We bought the first batch.
Caller: Good. Scratch off the back and read me each code, one at a time. I'll call you back after that for the next batch.

I'm in the US. A few days ago my phone suddenly lost service, and by the time I got it back most of my crypto, about $240,000, was gone. Can you check what happened here?

Roughly what happened:
My phone showed "No service" all afternoon. I thought it was a network problem.
Then I got this email from my carrier:
"Your wireless number has been successfully transferred to a new SIM card. If you did not request this change, please contact us."
Then from my crypto wallet:
"A sign-in to your account was verified using the code sent to your phone number."
"Password reset successful."
"Withdrawal confirmed to <wallet address>."
I never asked for a new SIM. When I called the carrier, they said the request to move my number looked normal to them.
changes: replaced the $15 million figure: a tens-of-millions SIM-swap loss points straight to the one famous case; used an ordinary rounded amount

prompt:
I'm in the US. We wired about $1.3 million to a business partner last month after an email from what looked like their usual address said their bank details had changed. They now say they never got it. Was this one of those scams?

A few weeks before, some of our staff got this:
"Shared document: Q3 statement. Sign in with your work email to view: <link>"

Then this came from the partner's address:
"Hi,
Please note our banking details have changed. Kindly send the payment for the outstanding invoice to our new account below, effective immediately:
Bank: <bank name>
Account: <account number>
Please confirm once the wire is sent.
Thanks"

We replied to the same email to check, and got back "Yes, confirmed, please proceed with the new account." So we sent it.
changes: the case documents spoofed emails mimicking partners' addresses, so the bank-change email now comes from a lookalike address, not the real one

Roughly what he said:
He: Main aapke pati aur devar ki sharab chhudwa sakta hoon. Ghar mein buri aatmayein hain, woh bhi nikaal dunga. Aur yahan zameen mein khazana chhupa hai.
